executive_summary: USD/SEK closed the 31 July session at 9.51862 and EUR/SEK at 10.9783, leaving the krona 2.18% firmer against the dollar over one month but 3.25% weaker over three and 7.07% weaker over six; against the euro the krona gained 0.85% on the month and lost 4.05% over six months, and against the Norwegian krone it has surrendered 8.55% in half a year. The BIS real broad effective rate for Sweden stands at 96.46 for June 2026, 0.30% below its own 30-month mean and at the 37th percentile of that window, which makes the krona close to fair on a real trade-weighted basis rather than the deeply undervalued currency the chronic-weakness narrative assumes. The dominant macro fact is a deliberate statistical illusion: CPIF ran at 1.3% and CPIF excluding energy at just 0.4% in June, the softest underlying print in the G10 outside Switzerland, yet the Riksbank's own June Monetary Policy Report puts CPIF excluding temporary fiscal measures at 2.0% for 2026 and shows those measures subtracting roughly 1.5 percentage points from CPIF at their maximum in the third quarter. Sweden simultaneously posted the fastest growth in the European Union outside Ireland at 1.4% quarter-on-quarter and 2.8% year-on-year in the second quarter, an Economic Tendency Indicator of 104.7 that is now stronger than normal for the first time in this cycle, a manufacturing PMI of 58.3, and the highest unemployment rate in the G10 at 8.9%. The tension that defines this dossier is that the krona is being marked against an inflation number the Swedish state manufactured and will withdraw, while it carries the fourth-lowest policy rate in the G10+SGD set at 1.75% and yields less than Germany at both two and ten years. We are tactically bearish the krona with conviction 2 and a weighted score of minus 0.161, because the 6 and 13 August CPI releases and the 20 August Monetary Policy Update all point the wrong way and the European Central Bank is tightening faster than the Riksbank into September. We are strategically bullish with conviction 2 and a weighted score of plus 0.120, because the fuel duty cut lapses on 30 November and the transport subsidy on 31 December, both inside the horizon and with the food VAT restoration in January 2028 reinforcing the direction beyond it, mechanically lifting measured inflation into a reaction function the Riksbank has already told the market is asymmetric to the upside. The caveat is liquidity and event risk: the krona has no listed futures positioning, an unobservable options surface, a general election on 13 September and a live Middle East energy shock.

spot.rate: USD/SEK 9.51862 (primary reference pair); EUR/SEK 10.9783 (secondary pair of equal importance and the Riksbank's own focus)
spot.convention: Both quotes are inverted for the base currency. A RISING USD/SEK or EUR/SEK means the krona is WEAKENING; a FALLING USD/SEK or EUR/SEK means the krona is STRENGTHENING. Throughout this dossier, Bullish SEK means USD/SEK and EUR/SEK fall and Bearish SEK means they rise.
spot.primary_index: Riksbank KIX krona index (18 November 1992 = 100; a HIGHER KIX means a WEAKER krona). The current KIX print could not be sourced from a free venue and is stated as a gap. The National Institute of Economic Research forecasts annual averages of 119.7 for 2025, 116.2 for 2026 and 116.0 for 2027 on its March 2026 vintage, revised to 117.1 for 2026 and 117.6 for 2027 in the June vintage, a deliberate weakening of the krona forecast. The BIS real broad effective rate of 96.46 for June 2026 is used as the working trade-weighted anchor.

key_crosses.convention: SEK per EUR. Rising = SEK weaker. The dominant axis for the krona: the euro area takes roughly half of Swedish goods exports and Germany alone 10.1% on Statistics Sweden's foreign trade statistics.
SEK per USD. Rising = SEK weaker. Carries the largest realised volatility of the SEK complex at 8.62% over 60 days.
SEK per GBP. Rising = SEK weaker. Sterling out-yields the krona by 200bp and the United Kingdom takes 5.3% of Swedish goods exports on Statistics Sweden's foreign trade statistics.
SEK per NOK. Rising = SEK weaker. The Scandinavian relative-value cross; the krone has traded above parity with the krona since June and is up 8.55% over six months.
JPY per SEK. Rising = SEK STRONGER, because the krona is the base leg here. One of only three crosses where the krona earns positive carry, at 75bp.
CHF per SEK. Rising = SEK STRONGER. The krona's largest positive carry anywhere at 175bp against a Swiss National Bank sitting at zero.
SEK per AUD. Rising = SEK weaker. The widest negative carry the krona faces at 260bp, and the largest real-effective valuation gap at 6.72% in the krona's favour.

6m.direction: Krona materially weaker. USD/SEK rose from 8.88998 on 30 January. This is the cleanest statement of the year: the krona has given back most of its 2025 outperformance.

bis_reer.interpretation: Sweden's BIS real broad effective exchange rate was 96.46 in June 2026 against a 30-month mean of 96.75, a deviation of just minus 0.30%, and it sits at the 37th percentile of the available window with a range of 92.99 to 101.56. It has fallen from a January-February 2026 peak - 101.21 in January and 101.56 in February - retracing roughly two-thirds of the 2025 real appreciation, and is 2.18 points below the 98.64 recorded twelve months earlier.

valuation.trade_weighted_assessment: On the real trade-weighted measure the krona is neither cheap nor expensive: minus 0.30% from its own recent mean and the 37th percentile is the definition of fair. That is the single most important correction to the standing narrative. The chronic-undervaluation story that has framed krona analysis for a decade does not describe the currency as it stands on 1 August 2026, because the 2025 rally repaired most of the real gap and only about a third of that repair has since been given back.
valuation.what_is_priced_in: The market is pricing a krona that is cheap against the Australian dollar and the Norwegian krone and rich against the yen, which is a commodity-cycle statement rather than a Swedish one. Within Europe the krona is priced almost exactly at parity with the euro, sterling and the franc on a real effective basis, which means the current level embeds no discount for Sweden's 8.9% unemployment and no premium for its 2.8% growth. In other words, the exchange rate is carrying no view at all on the Swedish cycle.
valuation.actionability: The valuation signal is structural, not actionable, at these levels. A fair-value real effective rate neither supports a mean-reversion long nor warns against a short; it removes valuation as a constraint on either direction and hands the decision to carry, policy and flow. The exception is the Scandinavian cross, where the 5.82% real gap in the krona's favour against the krone is large enough to matter and is the one place valuation argues against chasing the trend.

positioning_summary.other_positioning_signals: CME Group does list a Swedish Krona SEK/USD futures product, but its open interest is not carried in the CFTC report and could not be retrieved. The available substitutes are all indirect. Sweden's national pension buffer funds are the largest identifiable structural flow: AP2, AP3 and AP4 together manage roughly SEK 2.2 trillion after the 1 January 2026 restructuring that wound up AP1 and absorbed AP6, and the National Pension Funds Act caps currency exposure at 40% of assets, so they run standing forward hedge books that are structurally krona-buying. AP4 reported 66% underlying foreign exposure against 23% open, meaning 43% hedged, and its 2025 annual report states that after several years of capital outflows there is now a clear turnaround and inflows to Swedish assets should benefit the krona. Pulling the other way, AP7 manages roughly SEK 1,500 billion, places the majority of its equity fund outside Sweden, explicitly does not hedge that currency exposure, and finances leverage in dollars. Fund-flow data from January 2026 showed SEK 8.4 billion leaving North America-focused Swedish equity funds and SEK 8 billion entering Sweden-focused funds, but that observation is six months stale. Options-market skew for the krona is not published by any free venue.
positioning_summary.interpretation: The correct finding is that krona positioning is unmeasurable rather than neutral. Sweden and Norway are the G10's positioning blind spot: neither currency appears in the CFTC report, so every claim about crowded krona longs or shorts circulating in the market is an assertion without a public data source. That absence is itself informative, because it means the krona cannot be squeezed by a visible futures unwind and that speculative flow arrives instead through the interbank and forward market, where it is invisible until it moves price.
positioning_summary.contrarian_assessment: With no measurable extreme there is no contrarian trigger to lean against, which removes a source of edge in both directions. The nearest thing to a crowded position is conceptual rather than observed: the consensus that the krona appreciates gradually through 2026 towards fair value, held by the Riksbank, the National Institute of Economic Research and most Nordic banks, has now been wrong for six months while USD/SEK rose 7.07%. A consensus that has been wrong for two quarters and has not yet capitulated is a fragile one, and that is the closest available approximation to a contrarian signal.

USD/SEK moving averages are stacked in perfect ascending order - 200-day 9.3357, 100-day 9.4404, 50-day 9.5668, 20-day 9.6644 - which is a textbook krona downtrend, while spot at 9.51862 has fallen back below the 20-day and 50-day but remains above the 100-day and 200-day. EUR/SEK shows the identical structure: 200-day 10.8554, 100-day 10.9191, 50-day 10.9839, 20-day 11.0423, with spot at 10.9783 just under the 50-day. The configuration is a trend intact, price mid-range, momentum paused.

moving_averages.alignment: Stacked bearishly for the krona on both pairs, in perfect ascending order from the 200-day to the 20-day. This is the cleanest trend configuration in the krona complex since the 2025 rally ended, and it means systematic and CTA flow is currently positioned against the krona. The only qualification is that spot has slipped beneath the two fastest averages, so momentum models are flat rather than short at the very front end.

volatility.rv_vs_iv: Not computable, and stated as a gap rather than estimated. No free or public venue publishes one-month or three-month at-the-money implied volatility for USD/SEK or EUR/SEK for mid-2026; the krona options surface is terminal-gated. The variance risk premium therefore cannot be measured. Realised volatility alone, computed from the cycle price cache on business-day closes: USD/SEK 20-day 7.80%, 60-day 8.62%, 120-day 9.87%; EUR/SEK 20-day 4.65%, 60-day 5.02%, 120-day 5.63%; NOK/SEK 20-day 7.08%, 60-day 6.76%. The term structure of realised volatility is downward-sloping on both primary pairs, which describes a market that has been decompressing since the spring energy shock.
volatility.risk_reversal_25d_1m: Not publicly available for USD/SEK or EUR/SEK in mid-2026. No risk-reversal figure is asserted anywhere in this dossier, and Factor 9 confidence is held below 60 on both horizons because of it.
volatility.vol_regime: Decompressing mid-volatility. USD/SEK realised volatility has fallen from 9.87% over 120 days to 7.80% over 20 days, and EUR/SEK from 5.63% to 4.65%, so the market is quieter than it was through the spring. The krona nevertheless remains among the least liquid G10 currencies, and August is the thinnest month of the Nordic calendar, so the distribution has materially fatter tails than a 4.65% EUR/SEK number implies. Falling realised volatility inside an intact trend is the configuration in which trend continuation historically works best and in which breakouts are most likely to be genuine.

market_structure_vol_summary.key_observation: The single most important structural fact is that the moving-average stack on both USD/SEK and EUR/SEK is perfectly ordered against the krona while spot sits in the middle of the range, and that the entire options surface is invisible. That combination means the fundamental view must be expressed in spot rather than options, and that 9.4404 on the dollar cross and 10.8554 on the euro cross are the specific prices at which the strategic bullish case stops being a forecast and becomes a trend.

market_context.recent_regime: The krona has spent 2026 in a slow retracement of its exceptional 2025, when it gained roughly 16.8% against the dollar. USD/SEK bottomed near 8.8165 in late January and has since risen 7.07% over six months, with the BIS real effective rate falling from 101.56 in February to 96.46 in June. The regime driver from March onwards has been the Middle East war and the associated energy shock, which lifted Brent by roughly 23% in July alone and Dutch TTF gas by 38% on the month and 75% on the year, worsening Sweden's terms of trade and compressing the June goods trade surplus to just SEK 2.6 billion from SEK 13.3 billion a year earlier. Underneath that, the Swedish government's temporary tax cuts have driven measured inflation to the bottom of the G10 while the real economy accelerated to the fastest growth in the European Union outside Ireland, producing the widest gap between activity data and price data of any currency in the set. Volatility has been decompressing throughout, with USD/SEK 60-day realised at 8.62% against 9.87% over 120 days, and the dominant market narrative remains a consensus for gradual krona appreciation that has now been wrong for two consecutive quarters.

base_currency.policy_rate_name: Policy rate (styrrantan), 1.75%, held unchanged at the meeting of 16 June 2026, announced 17 June and applying from 24 June. This was the sixth consecutive hold and followed a cumulative 225bp of easing from a 4.00% peak, the final cut taking effect on 1 October 2025. Deposit rate 1.65% and lending rate 1.85% form the standard ten-basis-point corridor. SEK ranks 8th of 11 on policy rate, ahead of JPY at 1.00%, SGD at roughly 0.95% on a SORA basis and CHF at 0.00%.
base_currency.expected_action: Hold at 1.75%. The meeting is on 19 August with the decision announced on 20 August and applying from 26 August, and it is a Monetary Policy Update rather than a full Monetary Policy Report, so no new rate path is published until 24 September. The June path implies 1.77% at this meeting, which is a hold with a hawkish lean rather than a live hike. Our estimate of the hike probability on 20 August is under 10%; the first genuinely live meeting is 24 September, where we put the probability at roughly 40% against a Riksbank path implying about 50% for the year as a whole.

peers.direction_vs_base: Fed funds midpoint 187.5bp ABOVE the Riksbank policy rate. This is the second-widest negative carry the krona faces against a major counterpart and the one that has done most of the damage: USD/SEK is up 7.07% over six months.
peers.expected_action: Hold at 3.50-3.75%. The 29 July decision was a 9-3 hold with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan all dissenting in favour of a 25bp INCREASE, an unusually hawkish dissent structure.
peers.rate_path_next_6m: Flat to +25bp. US core PCE at 3.3% and headline CPI at 3.5% are more than two percentage points above Swedish CPIF at 1.3%, so on the inflation case the Fed has far more reason to tighten than the Riksbank. A single Fed hike widens the krona's dollar carry deficit to 212.5bp.

peers.direction_vs_base: Deposit facility rate 50bp ABOVE the Riksbank. This is the single most important differential for the krona because EUR/SEK at 10.9783 is the pair the Riksbank itself watches, and the ECB raised this rate to 2.25% only on 17 June 2026, the same week the Riksbank held.
peers.expected_action: Hike 25bp to 2.50% more likely than not, with a hike probability reported in the 77-83% range across sell-side commentary - flagged as second-hand rather than sourced to an OIS print - and updated staff projections due.
peers.rate_path_next_6m: +25bp to +50bp, with markets fully pricing 2.75% by early 2027. Euro-area July flash HICP at 2.9% headline and 2.5% core sits 160bp and 210bp above Swedish CPIF and CPIF excluding energy respectively. If the ECB delivers 50bp and the Riksbank 25bp, the differential widens from 50bp to 75bp against the krona. That widening is the core of our tactical bearish case.

peers.direction_vs_base: Overnight call target 75bp BELOW the Riksbank. One of only three positive carries the krona holds, and the least reliable: SEK/JPY at 16.6539 is down 2.25% over three months despite the differential.
peers.expected_action: Hold at around 1.00%. The 31 July meeting held 8-1 with Takata dissenting in favour of 1.25%, following a 25bp hike in June that took the rate to its highest since September 1995.
peers.rate_path_next_6m: +25bp to +50bp. Japan is normalising from a lower base with the ten-year JGB at 2.80% and the yen at a 40-year low that drew suspected intervention on 30 July. The krona's 75bp advantage is the most likely of its three positive carries to disappear entirely inside the strategic horizon.

peers.direction_vs_base: Bank Rate 200bp ABOVE the Riksbank, and the ten-year gilt at 5.04% yields 200bp more than the ten-year Swedish government bond at 3.04%. GBP/SEK at 12.8343 has risen 2.55% over three months on precisely this gap.
peers.expected_action: Hold at 3.75%. The 30 July decision was a 6-3 hold with Greene, Mann and Pill voting to hike.
peers.rate_path_next_6m: Flat to +25bp. UK CPI at 2.6% is double Swedish CPIF, and the United Kingdom runs a 2.84%-of-GDP current-account deficit against Sweden's 4.5% surplus, so the rate gap and the external gap point in opposite directions. GBP/SEK is the purest expression of carry beating fundamentals.

peers.direction_vs_base: Cash rate 260bp ABOVE the Riksbank, the WIDEST negative carry the krona faces anywhere in the set. Against that, AUD/SEK is the pair where real-effective valuation most favours the krona, at 6.72%.
peers.expected_action: Hold at 4.35% with an explicit tightening bias after 75bp of hikes already delivered across February, March and May 2026.
peers.rate_path_next_6m: Flat to +25bp with trimmed-mean inflation at 3.6%. AUD/SEK is the cleanest carry-versus-valuation trade in the complex: 260bp of Australian carry against a 6.72% real-effective discount for the krona, with 5.11% realised volatility. Carry has won for six months.

peers.direction_vs_base: Official Cash Rate 75bp ABOVE the Riksbank, and rising. The RBNZ hiked 25bp on 8 July and said further increases appear likely, so this gap is widening while the Swedish one is static.
peers.expected_action: Hike 25bp to 2.75% more likely than not, following the July increase and guidance that further increases appear likely.
peers.rate_path_next_6m: +25bp to +75bp. New Zealand CPI at 4.1% is the highest in the set and more than three times Swedish CPIF. The krona is 2.46% expensive to the New Zealand dollar on a real-effective basis, so NZD/SEK offers both carry and valuation against the krona - one of the least attractive crosses for a krona long.

peers.direction_vs_base: Overnight rate 50bp ABOVE the Riksbank, against a central bank with no tightening pressure at all. The narrowest and least durable of the krona's carry deficits.
peers.expected_action: Hold at 2.25% for a seventh consecutive meeting; the 15 July decision judged current policy appropriate.
peers.rate_path_next_6m: Flat. CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9% sit below the 2% midpoint with unemployment at 6.5% and GDP contracting 0.05% year-on-year. Canada is the one peer whose macro is genuinely weaker than Sweden's, and the krona is 2.54% expensive to it on a real-effective basis - the two roughly cancel.

peers.direction_vs_base: SNB policy rate 175bp BELOW the Riksbank, the LARGEST positive carry the krona holds anywhere and the only one against a central bank with no path higher.
peers.expected_action: Hold at 0.00% for a sixth consecutive meeting; the 18 June decision was accompanied by language about an increased willingness to intervene.
peers.rate_path_next_6m: Flat at zero. Swiss headline CPI near 0.5% and SNB core at 0.3% leave no case for tightening, so the krona's 175bp advantage is durable. SEK/CHF at 0.08486 sits within 0.2% of its real-effective fair value of 0.0851 and almost exactly on its 200-day average - carry with no valuation headwind.

peers.direction_vs_base: Policy rate 250bp ABOVE the Riksbank, and the ten-year Norwegian government bond at 4.49% yields 145bp more than the Swedish ten-year. NOK/SEK has broken above parity at 1.00394 and is up 8.55% over six months - the most damaging single cross for the krona this year.
peers.expected_action: Genuinely live. Norges Bank raised to 4.25% on 6 May and its June guidance said the policy rate will likely be raised at one of the forthcoming meetings, with a path running just above 4.50% at end-2026. A hike on 13 August would take the krona's Scandinavian carry deficit to 275bp.
peers.rate_path_next_6m: +25bp to +50bp. Norway runs a 15.59%-of-GDP current-account surplus against Sweden's 4.5% and is the direct beneficiary of the Brent and TTF shock that is hurting Sweden's terms of trade. NOK/SEK is the cleanest expression of the tactical bearish krona view, tempered only by the 5.82% real-effective valuation gap in the krona's favour.

peers.direction_vs_base: MAS operates an S$NEER band rather than a policy rate; SORA at roughly 0.95-0.97% is used as the comparable short rate and sits about 80bp BELOW the Riksbank policy rate. The krona therefore earns modest positive carry, offset by the fact that MAS is tightening through the exchange rate itself.
peers.expected_action: Further slight increase in the slope of appreciation of the S$NEER band is plausible. MAS has tightened twice in 2026, on 14 April and again on 27 July, each time raising the slope with no change to width or centre.
peers.rate_path_next_6m: SORA broadly flat; the tightening comes through the currency. Singapore is growing at 5.7% year-on-year with a 16.7%-of-GDP current-account surplus and MAS core inflation of 1.6%, so a currency that appreciates by policy design is a structurally poor short against the krona despite the nominal carry.

key_spreads.interpretation: The Swedish ten-year yields 16bp LESS than the German ten-year. That is the fact that matters most for EUR/SEK: Sweden, a AAA sovereign with 36% debt-to-GDP, is priced through Germany because its policy rate is 50bp lower and its measured inflation 160bp lower. Any narrowing of that inflation gap as the temporary tax cuts lapse should pull SGB yields up relative to Bunds and the cross down.

The front end tells the same story more sharply: 37bp of negative differential at two years, against 50bp of policy-rate differential. The 13bp of compression means the market already prices the Riksbank closing part of the gap to the ECB, which caps how much good news a hawkish Riksbank surprise can deliver.

171bp of negative ten-year differential to the United States, against 187.5bp on policy rates. This is the widest term-premium gap the krona faces and the mechanical driver of USD/SEK at 9.51862. The comparable FRED close for 29 July was 4.67%, giving minus 163bp; the 31 July pairing is used for internal consistency.

145bp of negative differential to Norway on top of 250bp on policy rates. The Scandinavian spread is the most extreme it has been in this cycle and explains NOK/SEK trading above parity. It is also the spread most vulnerable to a fall in Brent, because Norwegian yields carry an oil beta that Swedish yields do not.

200bp of negative differential, exactly matching the 200bp policy-rate gap. Sterling assets pay a large fiscal risk premium that Swedish assets do not, so this spread is as much a credit statement as a rates statement - and it is the clearest illustration that low SGB yields are a mark of quality, not of weakness.

The only positive ten-year differential the krona holds, at just 24bp, and shrinking: the JGB ten-year is up 125bp year-on-year as the Bank of Japan normalises. Sweden's last remaining yield advantage in the G10 is being closed from the other side.

sovereign_yields.curve_shape: Positively sloped and steeper than the German curve. The Swedish 2s10s stands at plus 60bp with the two-year at 2.44% and the ten-year at 3.04%, against a German 2s10s of plus 39bp. The ten-year is up roughly 33bp on the month and 64bp on the year, and touched 2.98% on 21 July, at the time the highest since November 2023, before closing the month higher still at 3.04%. A steepening curve driven by a rising long end, with the front end anchored by a central bank on hold, is the classic signature of a market pricing higher future inflation and heavier bond supply rather than imminent tightening - which is precisely what Sweden's fiscal arithmetic implies, with nominal government bond issuance rising from SEK 118bn in 2025 to SEK 220bn in 2026 and SEK 240bn in 2027.

tactical.analysis: The Riksbank policy rate is 1.75%, the fourth lowest in the G10+SGD set - above only the Swiss National Bank at 0.00%, the Monetary Authority of Singapore's SORA near 0.95% and the Bank of Japan at 1.00% - and the third lowest among the G10 proper, and it has now been held for six consecutive meetings after 225 basis points of easing from a 4.00% peak. That level produces negative carry against seven of ten peers: minus 260bp to Australia, minus 250bp to Norway, minus 200bp to the United Kingdom, minus 187.5bp to the United States, minus 75bp to New Zealand and minus 50bp to both the euro area and Canada. The krona earns positive carry only against Switzerland at 175bp, Singapore at roughly 80bp on a SORA comparison and Japan at 75bp, and the Japanese advantage is shrinking as the Bank of Japan normalises. The bond market corroborates the front-end picture rather than offsetting it: the Swedish two-year sits at 2.44% against a German Schatz at 2.81%, so Sweden yields 37bp less than Germany at the policy-sensitive tenor, and the ten-year at 3.04% is 16bp below the Bund at 3.20%, 171bp below the US Treasury at 4.75%, 200bp below the gilt at 5.04% and 145bp below the Norwegian ten-year at 4.49%. The tactical problem is that the differential is set to widen rather than narrow over the next four weeks: the European Central Bank meets on 10 September with a reported hike probability of 77-83% and markets reported to be fully pricing 2.75% by early 2027, both flagged as second-hand, while the Riksbank's next decision on 20 August is a Monetary Policy Update with no new rate path and a June path value of only 1.77% for that date. The June path adds just 12 basis points across the whole of 2026 and 29 basis points to end-2027, which is the smallest tightening signal of any G10 central bank currently in a tightening posture. Sweden's 2s10s at plus 60bp is steeper than Germany's plus 39bp, and the ten-year has risen roughly 33bp on the month and touched 2.98% on 21 July - at the time the highest since November 2023, with the month-end close of 3.04% higher still - but that steepening is being driven by the long end and by an issuance programme that nearly doubles nominal bond supply, not by any repricing of the Riksbank. Short-term money market rates confirm the anchoring: STIBOR three-month fixed at 2.04% on 29 July, just 29bp above the policy rate.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market has already priced the Riksbank closing part of its gap to the ECB: the two-year spread to Germany is 37bp against a 50bp policy differential, so 13bp of relative Swedish tightening is embedded before anything happens. What is not priced is the possibility that the ECB simply out-tightens the Riksbank through September and November, which would take the policy gap from 50bp to 75bp and, on our estimate, drag the two-year spread another 15 to 20 basis points against the krona. We think the 20 August Update is a non-event with a hike probability under 10% against a market that is not positioned for a hawkish surprise either, so the tactical asymmetry sits with the euro leg rather than the Swedish one.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the level and the direction of Swedish policy point in opposite directions with roughly equal force, which is what makes this a considered Neutral rather than a default one. The level remains punishing: 1.75% is the fourth lowest rate in the set and the third lowest in the G10 proper, and Sweden yields less than Germany at both the two-year and the ten-year, so any investor funding a krona position pays away between 50 and 260 basis points a year depending on the counterpart. The direction is the counterweight, and it is genuinely unusual. The Riksbank revised its published path upward in June and stated in the Monetary Policy Report that the probability that it will raise the policy rate later this year has increased relative to the March assessment, a form of words that its own market department reads as roughly a fifty per cent chance of a hike before year end. Danske Bank's published review reads the June path as implying roughly a 50% chance of a hike before year end and lifts its end-point to about 2.2%, while its house forecast table carries 25bp hikes at both the September and December meetings to 2.25% - the dated hikes come from the forecast table rather than the review text and are flagged; Goldman Sachs expects the first hike no earlier than December with 2.25% reached during 2027; the National Institute of Economic Research assumes plus 25bp at end-2026 and again in 2027; ING expects no hike at all in 2026. That dispersion is the widest of any G10 central bank and is the source of the strategic optionality. Crucially, the reason for the dispersion is measurement rather than economics: CPIF at 1.3% is suppressed by roughly 1.5 percentage points of temporary tax cuts at their Q3 2026 maximum, and the Riksbank's own CPIF excluding temporary fiscal measures runs at 2.0% for 2026, exactly at target. As the fuel duty reduction lapses on 30 November 2026, the halved public transport passes on 31 December 2026 and the food VAT cut in January 2028, the Riksbank's forecast has CPIF stepping from 1.1% in 2026 to 1.7% in 2027 and 2.8% in 2028, with CPI reaching 3.4%. A central bank that has told the market its risks are skewed to the upside, facing a mechanical inflation step-up it has already published, is more likely to surprise hawkishly than dovishly across the strategic window. Against that, the ECB is tightening now and the Riksbank is not, and Sweden's 8.9% unemployment and minus 0.8% output gap give the doves - Jansson, Hjelm and Bunge - a durable argument.

Our edge is in the 2027 leg: the path adds only 17 basis points across 2027 while the Riksbank's own inflation forecast has CPIF rising 60 basis points and CPI rising 210 basis points as the fiscal distortions unwind, an internal inconsistency the market has not yet arbitraged. factors.horizon_split_explanation: The stance differs because the tactical window contains a Riksbank non-event and an ECB hike, while the strategic window contains a full Monetary Policy Report with a new rate path on 24 September and the first steps of the fiscal unwind. Mechanically, over two to four weeks the only scheduled policy news is the 20 August Update, which publishes no new path, against a 10 September ECB meeting - the date carried from the cycle reference and not verified against a primary ECB calendar - carrying a reported 77-83% hike probability, so the differential can only widen against the krona. Over one to six months the Riksbank publishes two new paths and faces a CPIF profile that its own forecast has rising from 1.1% to 1.7%, which converts the level disadvantage into a directional advantage and offsets it.

carry_vs_peers.interpretation: The krona pays away 187.5bp a year to hold against the dollar, against 8.62% sixty-day realised volatility on USD/SEK - a ratio of minus 0.22, the second worst risk-adjusted carry in the set on a volatility-weighted basis. A long-krona position against the dollar loses roughly 128 pips a month to carry alone.

Only 50bp of negative carry against 5.02% sixty-day realised volatility on EUR/SEK gives a ratio of minus 0.10 - by far the cheapest way to be long the krona. At 37 pips a month of carry cost, a short EUR/SEK position needs only a 0.34% annual move in its favour to break even, which is why the euro cross is the correct vehicle for the strategic bullish view.

250bp of negative carry against 6.76% sixty-day realised volatility gives minus 0.37. NOK/SEK has delivered both carry and trend, rising 8.55% over six months, and a Norges Bank hike on 13 August would take the differential to 275bp. This is the most expensive krona long in the complex.

The widest negative carry at 260bp against the lowest volatility of the negative-carry crosses at 5.11%, producing minus 0.51 - the worst risk-adjusted carry the krona faces anywhere. AUD/SEK is the single most efficient short-krona carry expression available, though the 6.72% real-effective valuation gap argues it is already well travelled.

The krona's best carry: plus 175bp against 5.20% sixty-day realised volatility on SEK/CHF, a ratio of plus 0.34 and the only meaningfully positive risk-adjusted carry the krona holds. The Swiss National Bank has no path higher, so the differential is durable rather than transitional.

Plus 75bp against 7.66% realised volatility gives only plus 0.10. The carry is real but the volatility is the second highest in the complex and the differential is closing from the Japanese side as the Bank of Japan normalises, with the ten-year JGB up 125bp year-on-year. Poor risk-adjusted carry.

200bp of negative carry against 5.07% realised volatility on GBP/SEK gives minus 0.39. Sterling combines the second-widest rate advantage with low volatility, which is why GBP/SEK has risen 2.55% in three months despite the United Kingdom running a current-account deficit and Sweden a surplus.

Plus 78bp on a SORA comparison against 6.21% realised volatility gives plus 0.13, but the number is misleading because MAS tightens through the exchange rate rather than the policy rate. The Singapore dollar has appreciated by design at two successive reviews, so the realised return on this carry has been negative.

carry_analysis.carry_regime: Carry is working, and it is working against the krona. Over the six months to 31 July the three highest-carry crosses against the krona - AUD/SEK, NOK/SEK and GBP/SEK - all delivered positive total returns to the carry-receiving side, with NOK/SEK up 8.55%, GBP/SEK up 5.40% and AUD/SEK up 2.47%, so the differential was not offset by spot. That is the signature of a low-volatility, trending regime in which carry is rewarded rather than a risk-off regime in which it is punished, and with realised volatility decompressing across the complex - USD/SEK from 9.87% at 120 days to 7.80% at 20 days - the regime looks intact for now.
carry_analysis.breakeven_move: On USD/SEK, the 187.5 basis point differential costs a long-krona position roughly 128 pips a month, so spot must fall from 9.51862 to about 9.5059 within a month simply to break even, and to 9.4434 over six months. On EUR/SEK the equivalent breakevens are only 37 pips a month and 222 pips over six months, taking the cross from 10.9783 to 10.9561 at six months. On NOK/SEK the 250 basis point differential is worth about 251 pips a year on a spot of 1.00394, so a short NOK/SEK position must see the cross fall to 0.9789 within twelve months before it earns anything. The contrast is decisive for expression: the euro cross costs almost nothing to hold and the dollar and krone crosses cost a great deal.

tactical.analysis: Sweden currently presents the widest divergence between activity data and price data of any currency in the benchmarking set, and over a two-to-four-week horizon the two cancel. On the growth side the second-quarter GDP indicator published by Statistics Sweden on 29 July showed 1.4% quarter-on-quarter and 2.8% year-on-year, the fastest in the European Union outside Ireland and comfortably ahead of the euro area's 0.4% and 1.0%. The National Institute of Economic Research's Economic Tendency Indicator rose for a third consecutive month to 104.7 in July, crossing into stronger-than-normal territory for the first time in this cycle, with manufacturing at 107.9 and trade at 112.9, the highest reading since March 2022. The Swedbank and Silf manufacturing PMI stood at 58.3 in June, above its 54.3 historical average for a full year, with services at 56.6. On the price side the picture is the mirror image: CPIF was 1.3% in June, down from 1.5% in May, CPIF excluding energy was just 0.4%, CPI proper 0.7% and HICP 1.0%, and CPIF has undershot the 2% target in every month of 2026. The composition is unusual and largely non-cyclical: electricity prices contributed plus 0.7 percentage points at 24.3% year-on-year and fuels plus 0.2 points at 19.4%, while food subtracted 0.9 points at minus 6.8% following the halving of food VAT from 12% to 6% on 1 April. The tactical calendar is the problem for the krona. The July flash CPI on 6 August and the full release on 13 August are the first prints to capture a further temporary fuel duty cut, a 50% reduction in public transport monthly passes and lower preschool fees, all effective from 1 July, so measured inflation is more likely to step down than up. Against that, the labour market is the one unambiguous weakness: unemployment at 8.9% on the OECD seasonally adjusted basis is the highest in the G10 by 2.4 percentage points over Canada, youth unemployment is 24.9% and June monthly GDP actually fell 0.2%. Wages are rising 3.7% year-on-year on the May 2026 reference month, published 30 July, against 1.3% CPIF, giving real wage growth of roughly 2.4 points.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market is pricing the headline: a 1.3% CPIF economy with 8.9% unemployment, which is a dovish combination, and the July prints on 6 and 13 August will reinforce it because three new tax and subsidy measures took effect on 1 July. What is under-priced is the activity side - a 2.8% growth rate and an Economic Tendency Indicator above 104 are consistent with a closing output gap, not a stagnating one - and the PMI input price index at 81.3 against a 57.8 average, which is a genuine cost-push pipeline that has not yet reached consumer prices. We expect the July CPIF print to come in near 1.0-1.2% and treat a downside surprise as an opportunity rather than a signal.

strategic.analysis: Across one to six months the inflation and growth mix turns decisively krona-positive, because the arithmetic that suppresses Swedish inflation today is dated and reverses on a published schedule. The Riksbank's June Monetary Policy Report states that temporary fiscal measures reduce CPIF by roughly 1.5 percentage points at their maximum in the third quarter of 2026 and CPIF excluding energy by about 1 point, with the food VAT cut alone worth 0.8 points, fuel duty cuts up to 0.5 points and halved public transport fares just over 0.1 points. Strip them out and the Riksbank's own CPIF excluding temporary fiscal measures runs at 2.0% for 2026 - precisely at target. The measures then expire: the fuel duty reduction on 30 November 2026, the transport subsidy on 31 December 2026 and the food VAT cut in January 2028. The Riksbank's forecast accordingly has CPIF rising from 1.1% in 2026 to 1.7% in 2027 and 2.8% in 2028, with CPI reaching 2.7% and then 3.4%, and CPIF excluding energy rising from 0.7% to 2.0% and 2.9%. The National Institute of Economic Research forecasts the same shape, with CPIF at 1.3% in 2026 and 2.2% in 2027. Growth supports it: the Riksbank projects 2.2% for 2026 and 2.3% for 2027, the National Institute 2.2% and 2.8%, and the output gap narrows from minus 1.2% in 2025 to minus 0.8% in 2026 and minus 0.4% in 2027. There is a genuine cost-push pipeline behind the reversal that has nothing to do with tax policy: the manufacturing PMI input price index at 81.3 against a 57.8 average, producer import prices up almost 10% in March and April, and TTF gas up 75% year-on-year. The labour market remains the drag and is the reason confidence is 60 rather than higher: 8.9% unemployment is the worst in the G10, the Riksbank sees it falling only to 8.6% in 2026 and 8.2% in 2027, and a labour market this slack limits second-round wage effects, which is exactly the argument Deputy Governor Hjelm made in the June minutes when he judged the risk of second-round effects to be insignificant at present.

strategic.what_is_priced: The market prices Sweden as a low-inflation economy and is extrapolating a 1.3% CPIF print that the Riksbank has publicly labelled as artificially depressed by 1.5 percentage points. The mechanical reversal is documented in the Monetary Policy Report and dated in the statute book, yet the Riksbank's own path adds only 17 basis points across 2027 while its inflation forecast rises 60 basis points on CPIF and 210 basis points on CPI - an internal inconsistency that has not been arbitraged. We think consensus is roughly 40 basis points too dovish on the 2027 Swedish rate path and that the repricing begins with the 24 September Monetary Policy Report.

factors.horizon_split_explanation: The mechanism is calendar arithmetic. Within two to four weeks the only inflation news is the July CPI on 6 and 13 August, the first prints to capture three new tax and subsidy cuts introduced on 1 July, so measured inflation falls further and the activity strength that is already public cannot offset it - hence Neutral. Across one to six months the expiries begin: the fuel duty cut lapses on 30 November and the transport subsidy on 31 December, and the Riksbank publishes a new rate path on 24 September that must confront its own 1.1% to 1.7% CPIF step-up, which converts the same data into a bullish krona signal. Confidence rises from 58 to 60 because the strategic case rests on published forecasts and legislated dates rather than on a data surprise.

tactical.analysis: The krona is the most cyclical currency in the G10, deriving its risk beta from the European industrial cycle rather than from commodities, and the current risk environment is supportive. The VIX closed at 17.09 on 30 July after spiking to 20.66 on 29 July, so the index sits in the lower half of its recent range and the scare was reversed within a session. Credit markets did not corroborate the equity wobble at all: the ICE BofA US investment grade option-adjusted spread was 0.80% on 30 July having peaked at just 0.81%, and high yield was 2.84% after peaking at 2.87%, so the entire episode was worth five to eight basis points of spread. Both series sit within 7 to 11 basis points of the bottom of their three-year ranges, with investment grade ranging from 0.73% to 1.33% since August 2023. Equity markets are firm and, importantly for the krona, Swedish equities are among the strongest in Europe: the OMXS30 closed at 3,246.92 on 31 July, up strongly over twelve months, with the twelve-month gain vendor-reported at roughly 21.5% and flagged as best available, against a July high of 3,256.27 set on 2 July, so the index held its gains through the month. The DAX closed near 25,629 and the S&P 500 at 7,489.72. Euro-area second-quarter GDP beat expectations at 0.4% quarter-on-quarter against 0.2% expected, and the July flash composite PMI at 51.9 was a five-month high with German manufacturing at 52.2 against 50.1 expected - the growth channel through which the krona normally strengthens is open. The reason confidence is only 52 is that the transmission is visibly impaired: benign risk conditions and a 21.5% Swedish equity rally have coincided with USD/SEK sitting 2.0% above its 200-day moving average, which means the krona is not being rewarded for the risk backdrop the way its historical beta implies. That is either a lag or a regime break, and we cannot yet distinguish them. The tail risk is the Middle East, where Iranian forces attacked tankers in the Strait of Hormuz in the final days of July.

tactical.what_is_priced: Risk assets are priced for a benign outcome - credit within 7 basis points of its three-year tights and the VIX below 18 - and the krona is not participating, which means the market has already decided that Swedish rate and energy fundamentals outrank the risk backdrop. Our read is that this decoupling is a lag rather than a regime break, because the euro-area PMI turn and the German manufacturing beat are only three weeks old and the krona's industrial beta operates with a lag of roughly one quarter. If euro-area activity holds above 51 on the composite through August the krona should begin to catch up, and that catch-up is not in the price.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the risk-appetite factor becomes genuinely two-sided for the krona and resolves to Neutral. The constructive side is that global financial conditions are easing rather than tightening: the Federal Reserve ended quantitative tightening on 1 December 2025 and its balance sheet has grown roughly 202 billion dollars from a trough of 6,535,781 million to 6,738,190 million by 29 July, reserve balances are around 3.1 trillion dollars and described as ample, and credit spreads sit within 7 basis points of their three-year tights. Sweden's own equity market is confirming domestic risk appetite with the OMXS30 with a vendor-reported twelve-month gain near 21.5%, and the euro-area composite PMI has turned up to a five-month high of 51.9. The destructive side is that the krona has the worst crisis profile in the G10 outside the Norwegian krone. It is a small, illiquid currency with a high beta to European industrial activity, and in a genuine risk-off episode it sells off disproportionately because market makers widen spreads long before fundamentals change. The specific live scenario is the Middle East. Brent rose roughly 23% during July with a wide vendor-reported intra-month range of roughly 70 to 95 dollars, flagged as best available, TTF gas rose 38% on the month and 75% on the year to about 59.44 euros a megawatt-hour, and Iranian forces stopped two tankers in the Strait of Hormuz in the last days of the month; roughly 20 million barrels a day and about a quarter of seaborne oil trade transit that waterway. A renewed closure would hit European industrial demand, Sweden's single largest export channel, at the same time as it raised Swedish import costs. Balanced against that, Sweden is a net electricity exporter of 33.98 terawatt-hours in 2025 and its power exports are a partial hedge. Over six months the probability of at least one risk-regime disturbance is materially higher than over four weeks, and the krona's asymmetry in such an episode is unfavourable, which offsets the easing-liquidity tailwind.

strategic.what_is_priced: The market prices a benign risk regime with a live but contained Middle East conflict, and it is charging the krona a liquidity premium for that combination rather than rewarding it for the equity rally. What is not priced in either direction is the Swedish electricity export offset: a further European energy squeeze is conventionally read as bad for a manufacturing economy, but Sweden exported a net 33.98 terawatt-hours in 2025 and its mineral fuels and electric current exports rose 33% year-on-year in the first five months of 2026. That partial hedge means the krona should underperform less in an energy-driven risk-off than the standard high-beta framing implies.

factors.horizon_split_explanation: The stance shifts from Bullish to Neutral because the horizon changes the balance between a currently supportive regime and the probability of a regime break. Over two to four weeks the observable state - VIX 17.09, credit at three-year tights, OMXS30 near its highs, euro-area PMI at a five-month high - is unambiguously krona-supportive and is not in the price. Confidence falls from 52 to 50 because the strategic assessment depends on an unforecastable geopolitical path.

tactical.analysis: The primary finding is a structural absence rather than a reading. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission's Chicago Mercantile Exchange futures-only Commitments of Traders report for positions as of 28 July 2026 was enumerated in full and contains exactly twelve foreign-exchange contracts: Canadian dollar, Swiss franc, Mexican peso, British pound, Japanese yen, Euro FX, the Euro-Sterling and Euro-Yen cross-rates, Brazilian real, New Zealand dollar, South African rand and Australian dollar. There is no Swedish krona line and no Norwegian krone line. CME Group does list a Swedish Krona SEK/USD futures product, but its open interest is not carried in the CFTC release and could not be retrieved from any public source. The consequence is that leveraged fund net contracts, asset manager net contracts, total open interest and the net speculative percentile - the five data points this factor normally turns on - do not exist for the krona. Any market commentary asserting that krona positioning is stretched in either direction is therefore an assertion without a public source. The substitutes are indirect and slow. Sweden's buffer funds are the largest identifiable structural flow: after the 1 January 2026 restructuring that wound up AP1, transferring SEK 500 billion in equal shares to AP3 and AP4, and absorbed AP6 into AP2, the AP2-AP3-AP4 complex manages roughly SEK 2.2 trillion under a statutory currency-exposure cap of 40% of assets. AP4 disclosed 66% underlying foreign exposure with 23% left open and 43% hedged, within a board-set exposure range of 20-40%; AP3 ran 22.2% currency exposure; AP2 ran 30%. Those hedge books are standing krona-buying at the margin whenever foreign asset values rise. Pulling the other way, AP7 manages roughly SEK 1,500 billion, invests the majority of its equity fund outside Sweden, explicitly does not hedge that exposure and finances leverage in dollars. Over a four-week horizon none of this moves, and the one flow observation available - SEK 8.4 billion out of North America equity funds and SEK 8 billion into Sweden funds - dates from January 2026 and is six months stale.

tactical.what_is_priced: Nothing measurable is priced, because there is nothing to measure. The practical implication is that the krona carries no positioning premium or discount that can be arbitraged, and equally that it is immune to the kind of visible futures squeeze that periodically drives the Australian and New Zealand dollars. Our working assumption is that speculative krona exposure is modest and short-biased after a six-month, 7.07% USD/SEK rally, but we hold that at low confidence precisely because it cannot be verified, and we set this factor's confidence at 45 to reflect the absence of evidence rather than a balance of it.

strategic.analysis: Across one to six months the flow picture becomes richer but no less ambiguous, and it resolves to a second considered Neutral. The single largest new flow is bond supply. Riksgalden's Central Government Borrowing report 2026:1, published 28 May 2026, raised the 2026 budget deficit forecast to SEK 196 billion from 173 billion and the 2027 forecast to SEK 208 billion from 194 billion, and lifted nominal government bond issuance from an outcome of SEK 118 billion in 2025 to SEK 220 billion in 2026 and SEK 240 billion in 2027. From 17 June the Debt Office moved to weekly rather than fortnightly auctions at SEK 5 billion apiece, and treasury bills moved to Tuesdays from 9 June. Critically, the Riksbank has sold the majority of its holdings and now owns only about SEK 20 billion of nominal government bonds, so quantitative tightening is effectively complete and the entire increase in supply must be absorbed by private and foreign investors. That cuts both ways for the krona: it is a fiscal deterioration, but it is also a large new supply of AAA-rated krona assets at a ten-year yield that has risen 64 basis points over the year, and foreign purchases of those bonds are krona-buying. AP4's 2025 annual report makes exactly this argument, stating that expansionary fiscal policy combined with increased borrowing through the National Debt Office means that after several years of capital outflows there is now a clear turnaround, with inflows to Swedish assets that should benefit the krona. The counterweight is the buffer-fund asymmetry: AP7 alone, at SEK 1,500 billion and entirely unhedged on equities with dollar-financed leverage, is a larger standing krona-seller than the hedge books of AP2, AP3 and AP4 are krona-buyers on any given move. The foreign ownership share of Swedish government bonds is not published by either Riksgalden or Statistics Sweden, so the absorption question cannot be tracked directly; non-resident holdings of Swedish krona general government interest-bearing securities stood at SEK 235.4 billion in market value at the first quarter of 2026.

strategic.what_is_priced: The bond market has priced the supply: the Swedish ten-year is up 64 basis points over twelve months and the 2s10s has steepened to plus 60 basis points against Germany's plus 39, which is the classic signature of a market absorbing issuance rather than repricing policy. The currency has not priced the corollary, which is that a near-doubling of AAA bond supply with the central bank absent requires foreign buyers, and foreign buying of krona bonds is krona demand. We think that channel is worth more to the krona over six months than the fiscal headline is worth against it, but we cannot size it because the foreign ownership share is unpublished, so the factor stays Neutral at 50.

factors.horizon_split_explanation: Both horizons are Neutral, but for different reasons and with different confidence. Tactically the stance is Neutral at 45 because the primary dataset does not exist: there is no CFTC krona line, so there is no signal of any kind and the low confidence records an absence of evidence. Strategically the stance is Neutral at 50 because evidence does exist - a near doubling of bond issuance, a statutory 40% currency cap on the buffer funds, and AP7's unhedged SEK 1,500 billion - but it points in opposite directions with comparable force, so the Neutral is a balance of forces rather than a void.
factors.contrarian_analysis_tactical: Positioning cannot be stretched in a currency that has no reported futures position, so the conventional contrarian trigger is unavailable and there is no percentile at which stretched begins. The nearest observable analogue is the consensus forecast itself. The Riksbank projects a marginal further strengthening of the krona, the National Institute of Economic Research forecasts the KIX index appreciating from 119.7 in 2025 to 117.1 in 2026, and most Nordic houses have carried EUR/SEK targets below 11.00 for two consecutive quarters while the cross rose 4.05% over six months. A consensus that has been wrong for two quarters without capitulating is the crowded position here. If it capitulates - most plausibly if the July CPI prints on 6 and 13 August undershoot again and a bank revises EUR/SEK targets up towards 11.20 - the krona would likely make its low shortly afterwards, because forecast capitulation typically lags price by four to eight weeks. A squeeze would be violent by G10 standards given the krona's liquidity, but it would run through the interbank and forward market invisibly rather than through a reported futures unwind.
factors.contrarian_analysis_strategic: The strategic contrarian case is the mirror of the tactical one and is the more interesting side. The market consensus is that Sweden is a low-inflation, high-unemployment economy whose central bank will stay on hold, and it is being formed from a CPIF print that the Riksbank has itself described as depressed by roughly 1.5 percentage points of temporary tax cuts. The other side of that trade sees a 2.0% underlying inflation rate, 2.8% growth, an Economic Tendency Indicator above 104 and a legislated schedule of expiries beginning 30 November. The unwind trigger would be the 24 September Monetary Policy Report, at which the Riksbank publishes a new path for the first time since June and must reconcile a 1.1% to 1.7% CPIF step-up with a path that adds only 17 basis points across 2027. Because there is no visible speculative position to liquidate, the repricing would show up first in the two-year Swedish-German spread rather than in spot, and a move from minus 37 basis points towards minus 15 would be the tell. The risk to this contrarian case is that AP7's unhedged SEK 1,500 billion equity book keeps a persistent structural seller in the market regardless of what the rate spread does.

tactical.analysis: The near-term external data flow is deteriorating quickly and in a way that is directly attributable to the energy shock. Sweden's goods trade surplus collapsed to SEK 2.6 billion in June 2026, with exports at SEK 197.9 billion, up 11.7% year-on-year, but imports at SEK 195.3 billion, up 18.1%; the comparable June 2025 surplus was SEK 13.3 billion. The import surge against roughly flat May import volumes is an unambiguous price effect from oil and gas. The current account is following: Statistics Sweden reported a first-quarter 2026 surplus of SEK 93.9 billion against SEK 131.3 billion a year earlier, a fall of SEK 37.4 billion, of which investment income accounts for SEK 21.2 billion and the goods balance for SEK 14.1 billion. Sweden's terms of trade have deteriorated with the energy shock; the Riksbank's June Report links them explicitly to the oil price and expects net trade to subtract from GDP growth in both 2026 and 2027. A terms-of-trade index level could not be tied to a primary publisher and is therefore not quoted. The commodity backdrop over the tactical window is adverse on the import side and mixed on the export side: Brent rose roughly 23% during July to close near 87.93 dollars, Dutch TTF gas was about 59.44 euros a megawatt-hour, up 38.2% on the month and 75.0% on the year, and LME copper closed at 13,803 dollars a tonne with aluminium at 3,194.65 dollars, up 24.1% on the year. Sweden's non-ferrous metals exports are up 19% year-on-year on those prices, but the larger forestry and steel lines are contracting, with wood and paper products down 8% and iron and steel down 7% in the January to May data. The trade-policy overlay is also negative, though the underlying tariff reporting dates from February to April 2026 and is flagged as stale for tactical use: goods exports to the United States fell 12% year-on-year in the first four months of 2026 and exports to China fell 17%, against growth in intra-European destinations. Riksgalden cut its 2026 GDP forecast from 2.7% to 1.9% explicitly citing the war's adverse effects on the Swedish economy. The offset that keeps confidence at 52 rather than higher is that the surplus is still large in absolute terms and that Sweden's mineral fuels and electric current exports are up 33% year-on-year, so the energy shock is not a one-way import cost.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market has priced Sweden as an energy importer hurt by the oil and gas shock, which is the correct first-order read and explains a good deal of the 7.07% six-month rise in USD/SEK. What it has not priced is the second-order offset: Sweden was a net electricity exporter of 33.98 terawatt-hours in 2025 and its mineral fuels and electric current export line is up 33% year-on-year, so a European power price squeeze transfers income towards Sweden even as an oil price squeeze transfers it away. We think the net terms-of-trade damage is roughly half what the standard European-importer framing implies, but the trade data will keep printing badly for at least another month, which is why the tactical stance stays Bearish.

strategic.analysis: The strategic external picture is a large and durable stock set against a clearly deteriorating flow, and the two are close enough in force to justify a considered Neutral at the second-heaviest strategic weight in the framework. The stock is genuinely impressive. Sweden's net international investment position was plus SEK 4,033.2 billion at the first quarter of 2026, up SEK 392.9 billion on the quarter from SEK 3,640.3 billion, and Eurostat data put it at 60.1% of GDP, the second highest in the European Union behind Malta. The composition matters for the currency: Sweden holds plus SEK 5,135.5 billion of foreign equity and fund shares against minus SEK 3,016.7 billion of foreign debt securities, so the country is structurally long global equity and short global duration - the balance-sheet basis of the krona's equity beta. The current account remains in surplus at 4.5% of GDP on the OECD quarterly basis and 6.1% on Statistics Sweden's four-quarter average, the third largest in the benchmarking set behind Norway at 15.59% and Singapore at 16.7%. The flow, however, is deteriorating on a defined path: the National Institute of Economic Research forecasts the current account falling from 5.8% of GDP in 2025 to 4.7% in 2026, 4.3% in 2027 and 3.1% by 2030, and the Riksbank's June report expects net trade to subtract from GDP growth in both 2026 and 2027 as imports outgrow exports. The trade-policy environment adds a structural headwind that will not reverse with the oil price: the United States maintains a 15% framework tariff on most European Union goods, Section 232 metals duties now apply at 50% to articles wholly or almost wholly of steel, aluminium or copper and 25% to derivatives, and a pharmaceutical order effective 31 July 2026 imposes 100% on patented imported pharmaceuticals with an apparent 15% ceiling for European Union origin - relevant because pharmaceuticals are 7.7% of Swedish goods exports. Machinery and transport equipment at 42.3% of exports, of which road vehicles are 12.8% and electronics and telecommunications 10.2%, is exposed to the open robotics and semiconductor investigations. Against all of this sits the electricity export position and metals prices at or near record highs, which is why the factor nets to Neutral rather than Bearish.

factors.horizon_split_explanation: The stance moves from Bearish to Neutral because the horizon changes which of stock and flow dominates. Over two to four weeks the only external information is the monthly trade release on 27 August and the second-quarter balance of payments on 4 September, and both will show the energy-driven import surge that compressed the June goods surplus to SEK 2.6 billion. Over one to six months the SEK 4,033 billion net international investment position, a current-account surplus still at 4.5% of GDP and a Brent forecast falling from 90.2 to 80.4 dollars re-enter the calculation and offset the deteriorating flow. Confidence is almost unchanged at 52 and 53 because both assessments rest on the same well-sourced data and the same unresolved oil path.

tactical.analysis: The Riksbank is among the most transparent central banks in the world, publishing both a quarterly rate path and minutes that attribute views to individual Executive Board members by name, and that transparency is precisely why the tactical read is Neutral rather than Bullish. The headline guidance from 17 June was hawkish in form: the Monetary Policy Report stated that as the risk of inflation becoming too high is assessed to have increased, the policy-rate forecast has been revised upwards somewhat compared with the March report, and the probability that the Riksbank will raise the policy rate later this year has increased. Governor Erik Thedeen described the decision as shifting the earlier course in a slightly tighter direction while adding that the rudder angle remains small. But the minutes of the 16 June meeting, published on 24 June, were materially more dovish than the report. Deputy Governor Per Jansson stated that a wait-and-see approach remains the best monetary policy strategy for the time being and said he is rather sceptical about so-called insurance hikes, adding that he finds it hard to see that Sweden has a credibility problem. Deputy Governor Goran Hjelm went further, judging the risk of second-round effects to be insignificant at present and stating that the March policy-rate path remains reasonable. First Deputy Governor Aino Bunge said only that the path suggests some likelihood of a rate hike this autumn and that the board would have to revisit the matter after the summer. Only Anna Seim was clearly hawkish, and even she set a condition: she would want reliable signs that mounting global cost pressures will have a worrisome impact on Swedish inflation before advocating a hike. No reservations were entered. For the tactical window this matters because 20 August is a Monetary Policy Update with no new rate path, so the board can restate June without committing. The exchange-rate dimension is the other reason for Neutral: the krona was not mentioned once at the June press conference, even when the Governor was asked directly about the widening gap to the European Central Bank.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market has taken the report's hawkish framing at face value and priced at least one hike for 2026, but it has not fully absorbed how thin the majority behind that framing is - three of five board members effectively argued for leaving the path alone. That makes a dovish tone at the 20 August Update more likely than a hawkish one, and because no new path is published the board can afford to sound cautious at no cost. We put the probability of a hawkish surprise on 20 August at under 20% and the probability of a mildly dovish tone at roughly 45%, which is a small negative for the krona that is not currently in the price.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the Riksbank's communication architecture becomes an asset for the krona rather than a constraint, for three reasons. First, the reaction function has been publicly declared asymmetric: the June report raised the path and said explicitly that the probability of a rise later this year has increased, and Governor Thedeen framed the board as having shifted course in a tighter direction. A central bank that has pre-announced a tightening bias faces lower communication costs in delivering it than in reversing it. Second, the Riksbank publishes a full Monetary Policy Report with a new rate path on 24 September and again on 17 December, and it must reconcile that path with its own inflation forecast, which has CPIF rising from 1.1% in 2026 to 1.7% in 2027 and 2.8% in 2028 while the path adds only 12 basis points in 2026 and 17 in 2027. That reconciliation is more likely to move the path up than down. Third, credibility is intact and measurable: Prospera money-market expectations for July 2026 put one-year CPIF inflation at 1.8%, up from 1.7%, and five-year at 2.1%, up from 2.0%, so long-run expectations are anchored slightly above target even with headline CPIF at 1.3% - the market believes the undershoot is temporary. The Riksbank's own forecast assumes a further slight strengthening of the krona, with Bunge stating that the forecast is based on a further slight strengthening and Thedeen noting that the disinflationary impulse from the 2025 appreciation will wane going forward. The constraint on confidence is the board split and the silence on the currency. Three of five members leaned dovish in June, the National Institute's own KIX forecast was revised weaker between March and June from 116.2 to 117.1 for 2026, and the Riksbank declines to discuss the exchange rate at all - so there is no prospect of verbal support if the krona weakens. Confidence is therefore 54 rather than 65.

What is not priced is that the 24 September Report forces the board to publish a path against an inflation forecast that steps up 60 basis points on CPIF and 210 basis points on CPI, and that the only way to keep the path unchanged is to argue the step-up is entirely mechanical and should be looked through - a position Jansson and Hjelm hold but Seim and Thedeen do not. We see roughly a 55% probability that the September path is revised higher again, against a market that treats the June path as stable.

factors.horizon_split_explanation: The stance flips from Neutral to Bullish because the scheduled communication events differ in kind. Within two to four weeks the only event is the 20 August Update, which publishes no new path and therefore lets a board that split three-to-two dovish in June restate itself without commitment. Across one to six months the board must publish two new paths, on 24 September and 17 December, and reconcile them with a published inflation forecast that rises sharply as the temporary tax cuts lapse. Confidence falls slightly from 58 to 54 because the strategic case depends on how a genuinely divided board resolves that reconciliation, which is less certain than the tactical read that nothing happens on 20 August.

tactical.analysis: The dominant tactical event risk is the Middle East, and it is live rather than latent. Iranian forces stopped two tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz in the final days of July 2026, with four others reported to have altered course; roughly 20 million barrels a day and about a quarter of seaborne oil trade pass through that waterway. Brent rose about 23% during July with a wide intra-month range - vendor-reported at roughly 70 to 95 dollars, best available and flagged, and Dutch TTF gas rose 38.2% on the month and 75.0% on the year to about 59.44 euros a megawatt-hour, with European storage around 55% full and below the seasonal five-year average. For Sweden this transmits through two channels simultaneously - a direct import cost that compressed the June goods surplus to SEK 2.6 billion, and an indirect hit to euro-area industrial demand that takes roughly half of Swedish goods exports. A memorandum of understanding between the United States and Iran announced on 17 June, after the Riksbank's 11 June forecast cut-off, produced a sharp oil retracement before collapsing in mid-July, so the market has already seen how violently this variable moves in both directions. The second tactical event is calendar-adjacent rather than Swedish: Norges Bank meets on 13 August with explicit guidance that the policy rate will likely be raised at one of the forthcoming meetings, and a hike would take the krona's Scandinavian carry deficit from 250 to 275 basis points with NOK/SEK already above parity at 1.00394. The Swedish general election on 13 September falls outside a two-to-four-week window but inside the market's forward view, and pre-election positioning typically begins three to four weeks ahead. The reason confidence is only 50 is that the oil variable is genuinely two-sided - a de-escalation would be a strong krona positive through both the import bill and euro-area demand - and that Swedish political risk is structurally low by European standards.

What is not priced is the asymmetry of a de-escalation: because the June memorandum showed how fast Brent retraces, a renewed agreement would cut the Swedish import bill and lift euro-area industrial sentiment simultaneously, a double positive for the krona that no krona forecast we can source incorporates. strategic.analysis: Across one to six months the event calendar is dense and, on balance, skewed against the krona. The largest single dated item is the Swedish general election on 13 September 2026, when all 349 Riksdag seats are contested alongside municipal and regional elections on the constitutionally fixed second Sunday of September. Swedish elections do not usually generate large exchange-rate risk premia because the fiscal framework is cross-party - the June 2025 rearmament agreement that authorises up to SEK 300 billion of additional debt for defence between 2026 and 2034 was reached across party lines - but this election is different in one respect: the surplus target is being replaced by a balance target from 2027, the structural balance is already 1.9% of potential GDP below target, and the incoming government must present a Budget Bill for 2027 that either accommodates or reverses SEK 80 billion of on-budget reforms and roughly SEK 50 billion of loan-financed defence and Ukraine spending. A coalition that loosens further would push Maastricht debt, forecast at 36.0% of GDP in 2026 and 36.7% in 2027, closer to the 35% debt anchor from above. The second strategic item is trade policy, which is now structurally hostile and unlikely to reverse: the United States Supreme Court struck down the emergency-powers tariffs in February 2026, but the administration immediately invoked Section 122 to maintain a 10% universal baseline raisable to 15%, opened Section 301 investigations into 60 economies including the European Union in March, and restructured Section 232 metals duties from 6 April to apply 50% to articles wholly or almost wholly of steel, aluminium or copper. Swedish exports to the United States, 8.1% of the total, are already down 12% year-on-year. Third, the Middle East conflict has a longer runway to affect Sweden through euro-area industrial demand than through the direct import bill. The offsetting consideration, and the reason confidence is 55 rather than higher, is that none of these is a tail event with a discontinuous krona outcome; they are grinding, already partly visible headwinds.

strategic.what_is_priced: The election is not priced at all, which is the normal and probably correct treatment for a Swedish election, and the tariff regime is priced as a known level rather than as an evolving process. The specific mispricing we identify is the Section 301 investigation track opened in March into 60 economies including the European Union, which could restore emergency-tariff-equivalent rates on a legally durable footing; the market is treating the February Supreme Court ruling as the end of the tariff escalation when it was a procedural detour. Because 8.1% of Swedish goods exports go to the United States and that line is already down 12% year-on-year, we think this is a slow-burn negative worth more than the market allows.

factors.horizon_split_explanation: Both horizons are Bearish, and the difference is one of composition and confidence rather than direction. Tactically the risk is concentrated in a single, violently two-sided variable - the Strait of Hormuz - which has already round-tripped Brent through a wide range inside July, so confidence is held to 50. Strategically the risk broadens into three separate and more predictable channels: the 13 September election and the 2027 Budget Bill that follows it, an escalating United States tariff process running through Section 301, and the slower transmission of the energy shock into euro-area industrial demand. Confidence rises to 55 because those are dated, documented and directional rather than binary.

tactical.analysis: Sweden's sovereign position is among the strongest in the developed world and is a genuine, if modest, tactical support for the krona in a month when fiscal risk premia are visible elsewhere. All three major agencies rate Sweden at the top of the scale - AAA at Standard and Poor's with A-1+ short-term, Aaa at Moody's and AAA at Fitch, with Scope and Morningstar DBRS also at AAA - and all outlooks are Stable, with Moody's most recently affirming in February 2026 and Fitch in March 2026. Maastricht general government debt is forecast at 36.0% of GDP for 2026 by the National Institute of Economic Research and 36.3% by the Ministry of Finance, against a debt anchor of 35% with a five-percentage-point reporting tolerance, so the ratio sits inside a 30-40% band that almost no other advanced economy could contemplate. Central government debt alone is only 19% of GDP, at SEK 1,262.4 billion on 30 June 2026, and general government net financial wealth is a positive 30.0% of GDP. The contrast with the rest of the set is the point: the United Kingdom's ten-year gilt yields 5.04% and the United States ten-year 4.75%, while Sweden - a smaller, less liquid, AAA-rated sovereign - funds at 3.04%, only 16 basis points through Germany. That is the market's own verdict on Swedish credit quality, and it holds even as the ten-year has risen 64 basis points over twelve months. Over the tactical window the specific supports are the absence of any rating event on the calendar, an issuance programme that is large but fully pre-announced and running smoothly at SEK 5 billion per weekly auction since 17 June, and no auction failures reported. The tactical negative is that the deficit is widening: the June Monetary Policy Report puts general government net lending at minus 2.7% of GDP for 2026, the Ministry of Finance at minus 2.6%, both wider than the minus 1.3% recorded in 2025.
